blocks.text: General introduction and position in the periodic table

The d-block and f-block elements are the large central and bottom parts of the periodic table, where the electrons being added enter inner d or f subshells rather than the outermost shell. They hold most of the metals that built civilisation: iron, copper, silver, gold, titanium and the lanthanide-based magnets of modern devices.

Elements of groups 3 to 12 in which the last electron enters the penultimate $(n-1)d$ subshell. They are placed between the s-block and p-block and form four series: 3d (Sc to Zn), 4d (Y to Cd), 5d (La and Hf to Hg) and 6d (Ac and Rf to Cn).

An element that has an incompletely filled d subshell either in its neutral atom or in any of its common oxidation states. By this definition Zn, Cd and Hg (with $d^{10}$ in atoms and in their $+2$ ions) are not regarded as typical transition elements, although they are d-block members and share many properties.

Elements in which the last electron enters the antepenultimate $(n-2)f$ subshell. They are the fourteen lanthanoids (Ce to Lu, filling 4f) and fourteen actinoids (Th to Lr, filling 5f), usually placed in two rows at the foot of the periodic table, and are called inner transition elements.

The lanthanoids follow lanthanum (La) and the actinoids follow actinium (Ac). The fourteen-element rows are shown separately only to keep the table narrow; both groups really belong to group 3 in periods 6 and 7.

What to learn from this figure: the d-block sits between the s-block and the p-block in groups 3 to 12 and has four series (3d, 4d, 5d, 6d). The f-block elements (4f lanthanoids and 5f actinoids) are placed below the table and are called inner transition elements.

blocks.text: Electronic configurations of d- and f-block elements

In the d-block, the $ns$ and $(n-1)d$ orbitals have very similar energies, so the general outer configuration is $(n-1)d^{1-10}ns^{1-2}$. Palladium, with $4d^{10}5s^0$, is the notable exception. In the first series the 4s orbital fills before 3d in the neutral atom, but when the atom forms a cation the 4s electrons are removed first, because once the 3d orbitals are occupied they fall below 4s in energy.

blocks.caption: Electronic configurations of the 3d series (ground state)

blocks.text: **The two exceptions.** Chromium is $3d^54s^1$ and copper is $3d^{10}4s^1$ instead of $3d^44s^2$ and $3d^94s^2$. A half-filled or completely filled d subshell is specially stable because of symmetrical distribution of electrons and larger exchange energy, and the 3d and 4s energies are close enough for one electron to shift.

**f-block configurations.** The lanthanoids have the general configuration $[\text{Xe}]4f^{1-14}5d^{0-1}6s^2$ and the actinoids $[\text{Rn}]5f^{1-14}6d^{0-1}7s^2$. In lanthanum itself the 5d orbital is occupied; in gadolinium ($4f^75d^16s^2$) the half-filled 4f subshell is retained and one electron goes to 5d, and lutetium ($4f^{14}5d^16s^2$) has a full 4f subshell.

When writing the configuration of an ion such as $\text{Fe}^{2+}$, remove the 4s electrons first: Fe is $3d^64s^2$, so $\text{Fe}^{2+}$ is $3d^6$ and $\text{Fe}^{3+}$ is $3d^5$. Writing $3d^44s^2$ for $\text{Fe}^{2+}$ is a very common error.
Physical properties of the transition elements

The d-block elements are all metals. They are hard, lustrous, good conductors of heat and electricity, and malleable and ductile. Except for mercury, which is a liquid, and a few others (Zn, Cd and Hg are soft with low melting points), they have high melting and boiling points, high densities and large enthalpies of atomisation.

The reason is the unusually strong metallic bonding. Along with the $ns$ electrons, the unpaired $(n-1)d$ electrons also take part in bonding, so there are more bonding electrons per atom than in an s-block metal. The strength of bonding, and with it the melting point and the enthalpy of atomisation, rises as the number of unpaired d electrons rises, reaches a maximum near the middle of each series (around $d^5$), and then falls as the electrons begin to pair. Tungsten, in the 5d series, has the highest melting point of all metals (about 3700 K). Zinc, cadmium and mercury have fully filled d subshells, no d electrons for bonding, and hence low melting points.

blocks.caption: Trends in physical properties along a 3d series
rows: Melting point and enthalpy of atomisation
Rise to a maximum near Cr, then fall; Zn is low
More unpaired d electrons give stronger metallic bonds; filled $d^{10}$ cannot bond
Atomic mass grows while size stays nearly constant

blocks.text: Atomic and ionic sizes and the lanthanoid contraction

Across a 3d series from left to right the atomic radius first decreases, then stays almost constant, and finally increases slightly towards the end (Cu and Zn). Each added electron enters the inner $(n-1)d$ subshell. The d electrons shield the nuclear charge only imperfectly, so the effective nuclear charge on the outer 4s electrons rises slowly, which shrinks the atom. In the middle of the series the shrinking effect of the growing nuclear charge is balanced by the repulsion between the electrons in the d subshell, so the radii change very little. At the end the repulsion in the $d^{10}$ configuration wins and the radius rises a little.

What to learn from this figure: the radius falls, levels off and then rises slightly. The added d electrons shield the outer 4s electrons only poorly, so the radius falls at first; in the middle the extra d-electron repulsion balances the nuclear pull; at the end the filled $d^{10}$ set repels strongly and the size rises a little.

Moving down a group, atomic radius should increase. It does from the 3d to the 4d series. But the 4d and 5d members of a group (Zr and Hf, Nb and Ta, Mo and W) have almost identical radii, for example about 160 pm for Zr and 159 pm for Hf. The cause is the lanthanoid contraction.

The steady decrease in atomic and ionic radii of the lanthanoids with rising atomic number, from La to Lu (the $\text{Ln}^{3+}$ radius falls from about 106 pm for $\text{La}^{3+}$ to about 85 pm for $\text{Lu}^{3+}$).

**Cause.** Across the lanthanoids the electrons enter the 4f subshell. The shapes of f orbitals are very diffuse, and f electrons shield the nuclear charge poorly from the outer electrons. As the nuclear charge increases by one at every step, the outer electrons are pulled in progressively, so the size decreases steadily.
**Consequences.**

1. Elements of the second and third d-series in the same group (Zr/Hf, Nb/Ta, Mo/W) have almost the same size and therefore very similar chemistry; they are found together in nature and are very difficult to separate.
2. The third-series elements have higher ionisation enthalpies and are less reactive than might be expected.
3. The lanthanoids themselves are hard to separate by chemical methods because their $\text{Ln}^{3+}$ ions are so similar; the small difference in size is exploited in ion-exchange methods.
4. The basic strength of the hydroxides $\text{Ln(OH)}_3$ decreases from $\text{La(OH)}_3$ to $\text{Lu(OH)}_3$, since smaller cations hold the $\text{OH}^-$ more tightly.

What to learn from this figure: the 4f electrons shield the nuclear charge poorly, so the size falls steadily across the lanthanoids. This contraction cancels the usual increase in size on going from the 4d to the 5d series, so Zr and Hf have almost the same radius and very similar chemistry.

blocks.problem: Zirconium (4d series, group 4) and hafnium (5d series, group 4) have atomic radii of about 160 pm and 159 pm. Why is hafnium not noticeably larger than zirconium, although it lies one period below?
blocks.solution: Between Zr (period 5) and Hf (period 6) lie the fourteen lanthanoids, in which the 4f subshell is filled. Each 4f electron shields the nuclear charge very poorly, so for every extra proton in the nucleus the outer electrons feel almost the full extra pull. Over fourteen elements, the cumulative effect is a steady contraction in size (lanthanoid contraction). This contraction just offsets the normal increase in size expected from adding a new shell, and the radius of Hf comes out almost equal to that of Zr, 159 pm against 160 pm. The result is that Zr and Hf have almost identical chemical behaviour.
blocks.answer: The poor shielding by the 4f electrons causes the lanthanoid contraction, which cancels the expected increase in size of Hf.

blocks.text: Ionisation enthalpies

Ionisation enthalpies of the d-block elements are higher than those of the s-block elements and generally increase along a series, but the increase is small and irregular compared with the p-block. The increase in nuclear charge is partly offset by the shielding of the 4s electrons by the added 3d electrons, so the first ionisation enthalpies rise only slowly from Sc to Zn.

Irregularities arise from the stability of particular configurations. Removing an electron from $\text{Mn}^{2+}$ ($3d^5$) is hard, so the third ionisation enthalpy of manganese is unusually high; removing the second electron from Cu (giving the $3d^{10}$ ion $\text{Cu}^+$ to $\text{Cu}^{2+}$) needs a lot of energy, so the second ionisation enthalpy of copper is high. Zinc has high first and second ionisation enthalpies because of its stable $3d^{10}4s^2$ configuration, and the third is very high because it must disturb the stable $3d^{10}$ core. The ionisation enthalpies of the 5d metals are higher than those of the 3d and 4d series, one more effect of the lanthanoid contraction, and this is why the 5d metals (Pt, Au, Hg) are noble.
Oxidation states

One of the hallmarks of the transition elements is the exhibition of several oxidation states. The ns and $(n-1)d$ electrons are close in energy, so both sets can take part in bonding. The oxidation states of a transition metal usually differ by one unit, for example $\text{Fe}^{2+}$ and $\text{Fe}^{3+}$ or Mn from $+2$ to $+7$, unlike p-block elements where the states differ by two (such as $+2$, $+4$ in Sn).

blocks.caption: Oxidation states of the first transition series (most common states in bold)
rows: Only one state; loses all three outer electrons to reach $d^0$
$\text{Cr}^{3+}$ is very stable; +6 in chromate and dichromate
$\text{Co}^{3+}$ strongly oxidising unless in a complex

blocks.text: Moving across the series, the maximum oxidation state first rises to a peak at Mn (+7, equal to the total of 4s and 3d electrons) and then falls, because the d electrons become increasingly involved in the nuclear attraction and are not available for bonding. The highest oxidation state equals the group number up to group 7, and in the heavier elements Ru and Os reach $+8$ in $\text{RuO}_4$ and $\text{OsO}_4$. Lower oxidation states, even zero, occur in compounds with ligands such as CO, which accept electron density back from the metal.

What to learn from this figure: the number of oxidation states and the highest state rise from Sc to a maximum at Mn (+7) and then fall, because the d electrons become less available for bonding. Elements at either end (Sc, Zn) show only one common state, and neighbouring states differ by one unit.

**Stability.** Within a group, the higher oxidation states become more stable as one goes down (unlike the p-block, where the lower state is favoured by the inert pair effect). Thus $\text{Mo(VI)}$ and $\text{W(VI)}$ are more stable than $\text{Cr(VI)}$, which is a strong oxidising agent. Cu(I) disproportionates in water: $2\text{Cu}^+ \rightarrow \text{Cu}^{2+} + \text{Cu}$.

blocks.problem: Calculate the oxidation state of the transition metal in (a) $\text{K}_2\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7$, (b) $\text{KMnO}_4$, (c) $\text{K}_2\text{MnO}_4$ and (d) $\text{K}_4[\text{Fe(CN)}_6]$.
blocks.solution: (a) Let Cr be $x$. $2(+1) + 2x + 7(-2) = 0$, so $2x = 12$ and $x = +6$. (b) $(+1) + x + 4(-2) = 0$, so $x = +7$. (c) $2(+1) + x + 4(-2) = 0$, so $x = +6$. (d) The complex ion is $[\text{Fe(CN)}_6]^{4-}$; with four $\text{K}^+$ the charge on the anion is $-4$. $x + 6(-1) = -4$, so $x = +2$.

blocks.text: Standard electrode potentials, stability of higher oxidation states and chemical reactivity

The standard electrode potential $E^\circ$ measures the tendency of an ion to be reduced; a more positive value means a stronger oxidising ion and a more negative one means a stronger reducing metal. The $E^\circ(\text{M}^{2+}/\text{M})$ values in the first transition series decide whether the metal can liberate hydrogen from acids and how readily it is oxidised.

blocks.caption: Standard electrode potentials of the 3d series (volts, at 298 K)

blocks.text: **Trend for $\text{M}^{2+}/\text{M}$.** The values are mostly negative, and become less negative with irregularities along the series. Copper is the only one with a positive value, because the energy needed for sublimation and ionisation is not compensated by the hydration enthalpy of $\text{Cu}^{2+}$. As a result copper does not liberate hydrogen from dilute acids, whereas Zn, Fe, Ni and others do. Zinc and manganese show more negative values than the trend predicts, because $\text{Zn}^{2+}$ has the stable $3d^{10}$ configuration and $\text{Mn}^{2+}$ the stable half-filled $3d^5$ configuration.

**Trend for $\text{M}^{3+}/\text{M}^{2+}$.** The very positive value for $\text{Mn}^{3+}/\text{Mn}^{2+}$ (+1.57 V) shows that $\text{Mn}^{3+}$ is a strong oxidising agent and $\text{Mn}^{2+}$ ($d^5$) is very stable. The low value for $\text{Cr}^{3+}/\text{Cr}^{2+}$ (-0.41 V) shows that $\text{Cr}^{3+}$ is stable (its $d^3$ configuration is especially stable in octahedral fields) and $\text{Cr}^{2+}$ is a strong reducing agent. $\text{Fe}^{3+}/\text{Fe}^{2+}$ at +0.77 V is moderate, while $\text{Co}^{3+}/\text{Co}^{2+}$ at +1.97 V means free $\text{Co}^{3+}$ oxidises water.

**Stability of higher oxidation states.** The highest oxidation states are best stabilised by the most electronegative and smallest elements, fluorine and oxygen. Fluorine stabilises states such as $\text{VF}_5$ and $\text{CrF}_6$, while oxygen stabilises even higher states in the oxides and oxoanions $\text{VO}_4^{3-}$, $\text{CrO}_4^{2-}$, $\text{MnO}_4^-$; the compound $\text{MnF}_7$ is not known, but $\text{Mn}_2\text{O}_7$ and $\text{MnO}_4^-$ are. Oxygen can form multiple bonds ($\text{M}=\text{O}$) with the metal, which fluorine cannot, and this is why oxygen stabilises the highest states better.

**Chemical reactivity.** Transition metals are less reactive than s-block metals. Most dissolve in dilute non-oxidising acids to give hydrogen (the $E^\circ$ values are negative), except Cu, which is attacked only by oxidising acids. Some, such as chromium, resist attack because of a protective oxide film, and the 5d metals (Pt, Au) are very unreactive because of their high ionisation enthalpies and low hydration enthalpies. The $E^\circ$ values thus predict both the reactivity of the metals and the oxidising or reducing power of their ions.

blocks.problem: Using $E^\circ(\text{MnO}_4^-/\text{Mn}^{2+}) = +1.51$ V and $E^\circ(\text{Fe}^{3+}/\text{Fe}^{2+}) = +0.77$ V, calculate $E^\circ_{cell}$ and $\Delta G^\circ$ for the reaction $\text{MnO}_4^- + 8\text{H}^+ + 5\text{Fe}^{2+} \rightarrow \text{Mn}^{2+} + 5\text{Fe}^{3+} + 4\text{H}_2\text{O}$. ($F = 96500$ C mol$^{-1}$.)
blocks.solution: The oxidising couple (cathode) is $\text{MnO}_4^-/\text{Mn}^{2+}$ and the reducing couple (anode) is $\text{Fe}^{3+}/\text{Fe}^{2+}$, so $E^\circ_{cell} = 1.51 - 0.77 = 0.74$ V. Five electrons are transferred ($n = 5$), so $\Delta G^\circ = -nFE^\circ = -5\times96500\times0.74 = -3.57\times10^{5}$ J mol$^{-1}$. A positive $E^\circ_{cell}$ and a negative $\Delta G^\circ$ show that the reaction is spontaneous.
blocks.answer: $E^\circ_{cell} = 0.74$ V and $\Delta G^\circ \approx -357$ kJ per mole of reaction.

blocks.text: Magnetic properties

Most transition metal compounds are attracted into a magnetic field and are called paramagnetic, because they contain unpaired electrons. Substances in which all electrons are paired are repelled slightly (diamagnetic). Iron, cobalt and nickel are ferromagnetic: they are strongly attracted and can be permanently magnetised.
The magnetic moment arises from the spin of the unpaired electrons (the orbital contribution is small and usually quenched). For $n$ unpaired electrons it is given by the spin-only formula:
Here $n$ is the number of unpaired electrons and BM stands for Bohr magneton, the unit of magnetic moment.
Ions with $d^0$ ($\text{Sc}^{3+}$, $\text{Ti}^{4+}$) or $d^{10}$ ($\text{Zn}^{2+}$, $\text{Cu}^+$) configuration have no unpaired electrons and are diamagnetic.

blocks.problem: Calculate the spin-only magnetic moment of (a) $\text{Ni}^{2+}$ and (b) $\text{Fe}^{3+}$. State whether each is paramagnetic.
blocks.solution: (a) Ni is $3d^84s^2$, so $\text{Ni}^{2+}$ is $3d^8$. In $d^8$ two electrons are unpaired, so $n = 2$ and $\mu = \sqrt{2\times4} = \sqrt{8} = 2.83$ BM. (b) Fe is $3d^64s^2$ and $\text{Fe}^{3+}$ is $3d^5$, which has five unpaired electrons: $\mu = \sqrt{5\times7} = \sqrt{35} = 5.92$ BM.

blocks.text: Formation of coloured ions

Most compounds of transition metals are coloured in the solid state and in solution, whereas compounds of s- and p-block metals are generally white. The colour is the result of excitation of an electron between two d orbitals of the metal ion (a d-d transition). In an isolated ion the five d orbitals have the same energy; the surrounding ligands split them into two sets of different energy. A d electron can absorb visible light of just the right energy to jump to a higher d orbital. The light that is left, the complementary colour, is what we see.

The colour therefore requires an incompletely filled d subshell with vacant d orbitals of slightly higher energy. Ions with $d^0$ ($\text{Sc}^{3+}$, $\text{Ti}^{4+}$) or $d^{10}$ ($\text{Zn}^{2+}$, $\text{Cu}^+$) cannot undergo a d-d transition and are colourless. The colour also depends on the ligand, because ligands change the size of the splitting.

blocks.caption: Colours of some hydrated ions of the 3d series

blocks.text: The intense purple of $\text{MnO}_4^-$ and the orange of $\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7^{2-}$ are not due to d-d transitions: these ions have $d^0$ metal centres. Their colour arises from charge transfer from oxygen to the metal. This is a favourite exam trap.
Formation of complex compounds and catalytic properties

Transition metal ions form a very large number of complex compounds. The reasons are the small size and high charge of the ions, which give high charge density, and the availability of vacant d orbitals of appropriate energy to accept lone pairs from ligands. Examples are $[\text{Fe(CN)}_6]^{4-}$, $[\text{Cu(NH}_3)_4]^{2+}$, $[\text{Co(NH}_3)_6]^{3+}$ and $[\text{Ni(CO)}_4]$. The bonding between the ligand lone pair and the metal ion is a coordinate bond.

**Catalytic properties.** Many transition metals and their compounds are good catalysts. Two features account for this: the ability to exhibit variable oxidation states, so the metal can form unstable intermediates and shuttle between states, and the ability of the metal surface to adsorb reactant molecules and activate them, increasing the concentration of reactants at the surface and weakening the bonds in the adsorbed molecules.
Interstitial compounds and alloy formation

**Interstitial compounds.** Small atoms of non-metals such as H, C and N can be trapped in the empty spaces (interstitial sites) of the crystal lattices of transition metals, forming interstitial compounds. Examples are TiC, $\text{Fe}_3\text{H}$ and the iron carbide in steel. They are usually non-stoichiometric, so they do not have exact formulae, and are neither typically ionic nor covalent. The compounds are very hard, have high melting points (often higher than the parent metal), retain metallic conductivity and are chemically inert. The lattice becomes rigid because the interstitial atoms form bonds with the metal atoms.

**Alloy formation.** An alloy is a homogeneous solid solution in which atoms of one metal are randomly distributed in the lattice of another. Transition metals form alloys readily because their atomic radii are within about 15% of each other, so one atom can replace another in the crystal. Alloys are harder and have higher melting points and greater strength and corrosion resistance than the pure metals.

blocks.caption: Some important alloys
rows: About 95% lanthanoid metals, 5% Fe, with traces of S, C, Ca, Al
Lighter flints; Mg-based alloys for bullets and shells

blocks.text: Nature of oxides and oxanions of d-block metals

Transition metals form oxides in several oxidation states, and the character of the oxide depends on the oxidation state. A general rule is that as the oxidation state of the metal rises, the oxide changes from basic through amphoteric to acidic, because the higher the oxidation state the more covalent the M-O bond and the greater the polarising power of the metal.

blocks.caption: Acid-base nature of oxides of Cr and Mn

blocks.text: The oxides in the lower oxidation states are basic and dissolve in acids to give salts, while those of high oxidation states are acidic: $\text{CrO}_3$ gives chromic acid and $\text{Mn}_2\text{O}_7$ gives permanganic acid, from which the oxoanions are derived. **Oxanions** such as chromate ($\text{CrO}_4^{2-}$), dichromate ($\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7^{2-}$), permanganate ($\text{MnO}_4^-$) and vanadate ($\text{VO}_4^{3-}$) are formed by the metal in its highest oxidation states, and the group number is the oxidation state of the metal in them. These are good oxidising agents, because the metal is at or near its highest oxidation state.
Some important compounds: potassium dichromate and potassium permanganate

**Potassium dichromate, $\text{K}_2\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7$.** It is prepared from chromite ore, $\text{FeCr}_2\text{O}_4$. The ore is fused with sodium carbonate in excess air, which gives yellow sodium chromate:
The sodium chromate is extracted with water, filtered from the iron oxide, and acidified to give sodium dichromate.

Sodium dichromate solution is treated with potassium chloride; the less soluble orange crystals of $\text{K}_2\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7$ separate out: $\text{Na}_2\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7 + 2\text{KCl} \rightarrow \text{K}_2\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7 + 2\text{NaCl}$.

The chromate and dichromate ions are interconvertible by changing the pH. In alkaline solution the yellow chromate ion, $\text{CrO}_4^{2-}$, predominates; in acidic solution the orange dichromate ion is formed: $2\text{CrO}_4^{2-} + 2\text{H}^+ \rightleftharpoons \text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7^{2-} + \text{H}_2\text{O}$. The chromate ion is tetrahedral, and the dichromate ion consists of two tetrahedra sharing a corner oxygen, with a Cr-O-Cr angle of about $126^\circ$.

blocks.caption: Chromate and dichromate ions compared
rows: Medium in which it is stable
Two tetrahedra sharing a corner oxygen (Cr-O-Cr)

blocks.text: In acidic solution dichromate is a strong oxidising agent, its Cr(VI) being reduced to the green $\text{Cr}^{3+}$:

Six electrons are accepted per dichromate ion. Typical reactions: $\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7^{2-} + 14\text{H}^+ + 6\text{Fe}^{2+} \rightarrow 2\text{Cr}^{3+} + 6\text{Fe}^{3+} + 7\text{H}_2\text{O}$ and $\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7^{2-} + 14\text{H}^+ + 6\text{I}^- \rightarrow 2\text{Cr}^{3+} + 3\text{I}_2 + 7\text{H}_2\text{O}$.

**Potassium permanganate, $\text{KMnO}_4$.** It is prepared from the ore pyrolusite, $\text{MnO}_2$. Fusion with potassium hydroxide in air or with an oxidising agent gives the dark green potassium manganate, $2\text{MnO}_2 + 4\text{KOH} + \text{O}_2 \rightarrow 2\text{K}_2\text{MnO}_4 + 2\text{H}_2\text{O}$. The manganate is then oxidised, either electrolytically or by chlorine or ozone, to permanganate. In neutral or acidic solution the manganate ion disproportionates: $3\text{MnO}_4^{2-} + 4\text{H}^+ \rightarrow 2\text{MnO}_4^- + \text{MnO}_2 + 2\text{H}_2\text{O}$. Dark purple crystals of $\text{KMnO}_4$ result. On heating at 513 K it decomposes: $2\text{KMnO}_4 \rightarrow \text{K}_2\text{MnO}_4 + \text{MnO}_2 + \text{O}_2$. The $\text{MnO}_4^-$ ion is tetrahedral and diamagnetic, with Mn in the +7 state ($d^0$).
The oxidising action of permanganate depends on the medium:

blocks.caption: Reduction of permanganate in different media

blocks.text: In acid it oxidises $\text{Fe}^{2+}$ to $\text{Fe}^{3+}$, $\text{I}^-$ to iodine, oxalate to carbon dioxide ($2\text{MnO}_4^- + 5\text{C}_2\text{O}_4^{2-} + 16\text{H}^+ \rightarrow 2\text{Mn}^{2+} + 10\text{CO}_2 + 8\text{H}_2\text{O}$) and $\text{H}_2\text{S}$ to sulphur. Dilute sulphuric acid is used for acidification in volumetric work. Hydrochloric acid cannot be used, because $\text{MnO}_4^-$ oxidises $\text{Cl}^-$ to chlorine and the permanganate is wasted. Nitric acid is itself an oxidising agent and is also not suitable. Permanganate is used in titrations as its own indicator, since a single drop of excess makes the solution pink, and as a disinfectant and bleaching agent.

blocks.problem: 25.0 mL of an acidified solution of $\text{Fe}^{2+}$ reacts completely with 20.0 mL of 0.0200 M $\text{K}_2\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7$. Find the molarity of the $\text{Fe}^{2+}$ solution. (Use $\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7^{2-} + 14\text{H}^+ + 6\text{Fe}^{2+} \rightarrow 2\text{Cr}^{3+} + 6\text{Fe}^{3+} + 7\text{H}_2\text{O}$.)
blocks.solution: Moles of dichromate $= 0.0200\ \text{mol L}^{-1}\times0.0200\ \text{L} = 4.00\times10^{-4}$ mol. The equation shows 6 mol of $\text{Fe}^{2+}$ for each mole of dichromate, so moles of $\text{Fe}^{2+} = 6\times4.00\times10^{-4} = 2.40\times10^{-3}$ mol. This is in 25.0 mL, so molarity $= \frac{2.40\times10^{-3}}{0.0250} = 0.0960$ M.

blocks.problem: In an acidic medium, 20.0 mL of an $\text{Fe}^{2+}$ solution requires 25.0 mL of 0.0200 M $\text{KMnO}_4$ for complete oxidation. Calculate the molarity of the iron solution.
blocks.solution: The ratio is $\text{MnO}_4^- : \text{Fe}^{2+} = 1 : 5$, because each permanganate takes 5 electrons and each $\text{Fe}^{2+}$ gives 1. Moles of permanganate $= 0.0200\times0.0250 = 5.00\times10^{-4}$ mol. Moles of $\text{Fe}^{2+} = 5\times5.00\times10^{-4} = 2.50\times10^{-3}$ mol. Molarity $= \frac{2.50\times10^{-3}\ \text{mol}}{0.0200\ \text{L}} = 0.125$ M.

blocks.text: For titration numericals first write the mole ratio from the balanced equation: $\text{MnO}_4^-$ : $\text{Fe}^{2+}$ = 1 : 5, $\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7^{2-}$ : $\text{Fe}^{2+}$ = 1 : 6, $\text{MnO}_4^-$ : $\text{C}_2\text{O}_4^{2-}$ = 2 : 5. Do not confuse these.
f-block elements: lanthanoids and actinoids

The lanthanoids (Ce to Lu, following lanthanum) fill the 4f subshell and the actinoids (Th to Lr, following actinium) fill the 5f subshell. This section covers their general properties, their atomic and ionic sizes and their oxidation states.

**General properties of lanthanoids.** They are silvery-white, soft metals that tarnish quickly in air. Their hardness increases with atomic number (samarium is steel-hard). They have high melting points (between about 1000 and 1200 K) and are good conductors. They are highly electropositive, close to calcium in reactivity. They react with oxygen, halogens and sulphur on heating, give hydrogen with dilute acids and react with water to liberate hydrogen. Their hydroxides $\text{Ln(OH)}_3$ are basic. Most trivalent ions are coloured, owing to f-f transitions; $\text{La}^{3+}$ ($4f^0$) and $\text{Lu}^{3+}$ ($4f^{14}$) are colourless. Their magnetic properties are due to unpaired 4f electrons, and most $\text{Ln}^{3+}$ ions are paramagnetic.

**Atomic and ionic sizes.** Across the lanthanoid series there is a steady decrease in atomic and ionic radii, called the lanthanoid contraction, described above. The ionic radius of $\text{Ln}^{3+}$ falls from about 106 pm to 85 pm.

**Oxidation states.** The most common oxidation state of the lanthanoids is $+3$, which is reached by losing the two 6s electrons and one 5d (or 4f) electron. A few elements show $+2$ and $+4$, usually to attain a $4f^0$, $4f^7$ or $4f^{14}$ configuration. $\text{Ce}^{4+}$ ($4f^0$) is a strong oxidising agent, with $E^\circ(\text{Ce}^{4+}/\text{Ce}^{3+}) = +1.74$ V, and reverts to $+3$. $\text{Eu}^{2+}$ ($4f^7$) and $\text{Yb}^{2+}$ ($4f^{14}$) are reducing agents, going to the stable $+3$ state. Other $+4$ examples are Pr and Tb.

**Actinoids.** The actinoids are all radioactive. Elements after uranium are made artificially (transuranium elements). They are silvery metals, more reactive than lanthanoids, which react with boiling water to give a mixture of oxide and hydride and combine with most non-metals at moderate temperatures. Hydrochloric acid attacks all of them, while alkali has no action. Their ions are generally coloured, and their magnetic properties are more complicated than those of lanthanoids. The actinoids show an actinoid contraction similar to the lanthanoid contraction; it is greater from element to element because 5f electrons shield even less effectively.

**Oxidation states of actinoids.** The actinoids show a much wider range than the lanthanoids, because the 5f, 6d and 7s orbitals have comparable energies. $+3$ is the common state but $+4$, $+5$, $+6$ and $+7$ also occur. Uranium is found as $+3$, $+4$, $+5$ and $+6$, neptunium and plutonium show up to $+7$, and the $+3$ state becomes the most stable for the later elements.

blocks.caption: Lanthanoids at a glance
rows: Lanthanoid contraction: $\text{Ln}^{3+}$ falls from about 106 pm to 85 pm

blocks.text: Comparison of actinoids with lanthanoids

Both series are inner transition elements, and both show $+3$ as a common oxidation state, a gradual decrease in size (the lanthanoid and actinoid contractions), paramagnetism, high electropositive character and the formation of coloured ions. But they differ in important ways.

blocks.caption: Comparison of actinoids and lanthanoids
rows: Participation of f electrons in bonding
Greater, as 5f orbitals extend further out
Actinoid contraction, greater from element to element

blocks.text: The 5f orbitals extend into space more than the 4f orbitals and are therefore involved in bonding to a far greater extent. This is the root cause of the greater range of oxidation states in the actinoids.
Applications of d- and f-block elements

**Applications of d-block elements.** Iron and its alloys (steels) are the foundation of construction and machinery. Titanium and its alloys are used in aircraft and spacecraft, and $\text{TiO}_2$ is the main white pigment. Copper is used in electrical wiring and, as an alloy, in brass and bronze. Zinc is used for galvanising and in dry cells. Silver bromide is the light-sensitive material of photographic film. Nickel-chromium alloys (nichrome) are heating elements, and Ni-Cd cells are rechargeable batteries. Platinum, palladium and rhodium catalyse the removal of pollutants in catalytic converters. $\text{V}_2\text{O}_5$ catalyses sulphuric acid manufacture, iron catalyses ammonia synthesis and $\text{MnO}_2$ is used in dry cells. $\text{K}_2\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7$ and $\text{KMnO}_4$ are used in analysis, and $\text{KMnO}_4$ is used as a disinfectant.

**Applications of f-block elements.** Misch metal is used in lighter flints and in Mg-based alloys for bullets and shells. Mixed oxides of lanthanoids are used as petroleum cracking catalysts and in phosphors, europium for example giving the red colour of colour television screens. Neodymium is used in strong magnets and lasers. Uranium and plutonium are the fuel of nuclear reactors and the source of nuclear energy, and thorium is a potential nuclear fuel.

d-block: groups 3 to 12, $(n-1)d$ filling, variable oxidation states, coloured paramagnetic ions, catalysts, complexes, alloys and interstitial compounds. Zn, Cd and Hg are not typical transition elements.
Spin-only moment $\mu = \sqrt{n(n+2)}$ BM; $d^0$ and $d^{10}$ ions are colourless and diamagnetic; Cr and Cu have anomalous configurations $3d^54s^1$ and $3d^{10}4s^1$.

Oxides: basic (low oxidation state) to amphoteric to acidic (high). $\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7^{2-}$ (orange) and $\text{MnO}_4^-$ (purple) are oxidants; $\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7^{2-} \rightarrow \text{Cr}^{3+}$ (6e), $\text{MnO}_4^- \rightarrow \text{Mn}^{2+}$ (5e) in acid.
Lanthanoids: 4f, $+3$ common, contraction due to poor 4f shielding. Actinoids: 5f, all radioactive, many oxidation states $+3$ to $+7$.

questions.stem: The general outer electronic configuration of the d-block elements is
questions.explanation: In the d-block the last electron enters the penultimate $(n-1)d$ subshell, which has 1 to 10 electrons, while the outer $ns$ subshell holds one or two electrons. The configurations $ns^2np^{1-6}$ and $ns^{1-2}$ belong to the p- and s-blocks, and the long expression with $(n-2)f$ describes the f-block.

optionRationale.1: This is the outer configuration of the p-block elements.
optionRationale.2: This is the general configuration of the f-block elements.
optionRationale.4: This is the outer configuration of the s-block elements.

questions.objective: Recall the general electronic configuration of the d-block

questions.stem: Which of the following is not regarded as a typical transition element?
questions.explanation: A transition element has an incomplete d subshell in the atom or in a common oxidation state. Zinc is $3d^{10}4s^2$ and forms only $\text{Zn}^{2+}$ with $3d^{10}$, so its d subshell is always full. Fe, Ni and Cr all have partly filled d subshells in their common ions.

optionRationale.1: Fe has a partially filled 3d subshell in $\text{Fe}^{2+}$ and $\text{Fe}^{3+}$, so it is a transition element.
optionRationale.2: Ni has $3d^8$ in $\text{Ni}^{2+}$, an incomplete d subshell.
optionRationale.3: Cr has partly filled d orbitals in its atom and in its ions.

questions.objective: Apply the definition of a transition element

questions.stem:
Assertion (A): Transition metals show variable oxidation states.
Reason (R): The ns and $(n-1)d$ electrons have very similar energies and can both be used in bonding.
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).
questions.explanation: The $ns$ and $(n-1)d$ orbitals lie close in energy, so after the ns electrons are lost, d electrons can also take part in bonding. This produces a series of stable oxidation states, usually differing by one unit, such as Mn from $+2$ to $+7$. The reason therefore explains the assertion.

optionRationale.2: R is not just true; it is the cause of A.
optionRationale.3: R is true; the closeness of ns and (n-1)d energies is the cause of variable valency.
optionRationale.4: A is true; variable oxidation states are characteristic of the d-block.

questions.objective: Explain variable oxidation states in the d-block

questions.stem: The spin-only magnetic moment of $\text{Cr}^{2+}$ (atomic number 24) is closest to
questions.explanation: Cr is $3d^54s^1$. Removing two electrons (4s first and then one 3d) gives $\text{Cr}^{2+}$ as $3d^4$, with four unpaired electrons. $\mu = \sqrt{n(n+2)} = \sqrt{4\times6} = \sqrt{24} = 4.90$ BM.

optionRationale.1: This value is for five unpaired electrons ($\text{Mn}^{2+}$ or $\text{Fe}^{3+}$).
optionRationale.3: This value is for three unpaired electrons, as in $\text{Cr}^{3+}$.
optionRationale.4: This value is for two unpaired electrons.

questions.objective: Calculate the spin-only magnetic moment of an ion

questions.stem: The oxidation states of chromium in $\text{K}_2\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7$ and of manganese in $\text{KMnO}_4$ are respectively
questions.explanation: In $\text{K}_2\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7$: $2(+1) + 2x + 7(-2) = 0$ gives $x = +6$. In $\text{KMnO}_4$: $(+1) + y + 4(-2) = 0$ gives $y = +7$. These are the highest oxidation states of the two elements, equal to their group numbers.

optionRationale.3: Mn in $\text{KMnO}_4$ is +7; +6 is its state in $\text{K}_2\text{MnO}_4$.
optionRationale.4: Cr in dichromate is +6, not +3; +3 is the state in the product $\text{Cr}^{3+}$.

questions.stem:
Consider these statements about the lanthanoid contraction.
A. There is a steady decrease in atomic and ionic radii from La to Lu.
B. It is caused by the poor shielding of the nuclear charge by 4f electrons.
C. It makes the atomic radii of Zr and Hf almost the same.
D. It increases the basic strength of $\text{Ln(OH)}_3$ from La to Lu.
Choose the correct answer.
questions.explanation: The lanthanoid contraction is the regular decrease in size from La to Lu (A), caused by the poor shielding of the increasing nuclear charge by 4f electrons (B). It compensates the normal increase in size from the 4d to 5d series, so Zr and Hf are nearly equal in size (C). As the cations become smaller, the basic strength of $\text{Ln(OH)}_3$ decreases, so D is false.

optionRationale.1: D is false; basic strength decreases from La to Lu and B and C are also true.
optionRationale.3: D is false and A is true.
optionRationale.4: D is false and B is true.

questions.objective: Evaluate statements on the lanthanoid contraction and its consequences

questions.stem: Which of the following aqueous ions is colourless?
questions.explanation: Colour comes from d-d transitions, which need partly filled d orbitals. $\text{Sc}^{3+}$ has the configuration $3d^0$, with no d electron to excite, so it is colourless. $\text{Cr}^{3+}$, $\text{Cu}^{2+}$ and $\text{Ni}^{2+}$ have partly filled d subshells and are coloured.

optionRationale.1: It is $d^3$ and violet because of d-d transitions.

questions.objective: Predict colourlessness from the d-electron count

questions.stem: Match each hydrated ion in List-I with its colour in List-II and choose the correct code.
questions.explanation: Aqueous $\text{Cu}^{2+}$ is blue (A-II), $\text{Cr}^{3+}$ is violet (B-III), $\text{Mn}^{2+}$ is pale pink (C-I) and $\text{Fe}^{2+}$ is green (D-IV). In each case the colour comes from a d-d transition of the partly filled d subshell of the ion in water.

optionRationale.1: C and D are interchanged: Mn2+ is pink and Fe2+ is green.
optionRationale.4: None of the four matches is right.

questions.objective: Recall the colours of common hydrated d-block ions

questions.stem: Copper does not liberate hydrogen from dilute hydrochloric acid, while zinc does. The reason is that
options: copper has a very low ionisation enthalpy
copper forms a protective oxide film that dissolves in acid
the hydration enthalpy of $\text{Cu}^{2+}$ is very large and negative
$E^\circ(\text{Cu}^{2+}/\text{Cu})$ is positive (+0.34 V), so copper is a weaker reducing agent than hydrogen
questions.explanation: A metal liberates hydrogen from dilute acids if its standard reduction potential is below 0.00 V (the hydrogen electrode). Copper has $E^\circ = +0.34$ V, since its hydration enthalpy cannot compensate the sum of sublimation and ionisation enthalpies. It is thus a weaker reducing agent than hydrogen, whereas zinc ($-0.76$ V) is stronger.

optionRationale.1: Copper's second ionisation enthalpy is actually high; this does not explain its inertness towards acids.
optionRationale.2: A film is not the reason; the key factor is the positive electrode potential.
optionRationale.3: The hydration enthalpy of $\text{Cu}^{2+}$ is not large enough to offset sublimation and ionisation enthalpy; that is why $E^\circ$ is positive.

questions.objective: Relate E° values to reaction with acids

questions.stem:
Assertion (A): Zn, Cd and Hg are not considered typical transition elements.
Reason (R): Zn, Cd and Hg have low melting points compared with other d-block metals.
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).
questions.explanation: Zn, Cd and Hg have a completely filled $d^{10}$ configuration in the atom and in the common $+2$ ion, so they lack the incomplete d subshell that defines transition behaviour; this is why A is true. Their melting points are indeed low (Hg is a liquid), so R is true. But the low melting point is a consequence of the same filled d subshell, not the reason for exclusion.

optionRationale.1: The reason for exclusion is the $d^{10}$ configuration, not the melting point.
optionRationale.3: R is true: these metals have unusually low melting points.
optionRationale.4: A is true since their d subshell is always full.

questions.objective: Judge whether a true statement explains the exclusion of group 12 elements

questions.stem: 25.0 mL of an acidified $\text{Fe}^{2+}$ solution requires 20.0 mL of 0.0200 M $\text{K}_2\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7$ for complete oxidation to $\text{Fe}^{3+}$. The molarity of the $\text{Fe}^{2+}$ solution is
questions.explanation: The reaction is $\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7^{2-} + 14\text{H}^+ + 6\text{Fe}^{2+} \rightarrow 2\text{Cr}^{3+} + 6\text{Fe}^{3+} + 7\text{H}_2\text{O}$. Moles dichromate $= 0.0200\times0.0200 = 4.00\times10^{-4}$; moles $\text{Fe}^{2+} = 6\times4.00\times10^{-4} = 2.40\times10^{-3}$; molarity $= 2.40\times10^{-3}/0.0250 = 0.0960$ M.

optionRationale.2: This forgets that each dichromate oxidises six $\text{Fe}^{2+}$.
optionRationale.3: This uses a factor of 3 instead of 6.
optionRationale.4: This uses a factor of 12, counting both chromium atoms twice.

questions.objective: Do a titration calculation using dichromate

questions.stem: 20.0 mL of 0.0500 M $\text{KMnO}_4$ is just enough, in acid solution, to oxidise a sample of sodium oxalate. What mass of $\text{Na}_2\text{C}_2\text{O}_4$ (molar mass 134 g mol$^{-1}$) was present? ($2\text{MnO}_4^- + 5\text{C}_2\text{O}_4^{2-} + 16\text{H}^+ \rightarrow 2\text{Mn}^{2+} + 10\text{CO}_2 + 8\text{H}_2\text{O}$)
questions.explanation: Moles of permanganate $= 0.0500\times0.0200 = 1.00\times10^{-3}$. The equation shows 2 mol $\text{MnO}_4^-$ for 5 mol oxalate, so moles of oxalate $= \frac{5}{2}\times1.00\times10^{-3} = 2.50\times10^{-3}$. Mass $= 2.50\times10^{-3}\times134 = 0.335$ g.

optionRationale.1: This assumes a 1 : 1 ratio between permanganate and oxalate.
optionRationale.2: This uses a 1 : 5 ratio and ignores the 2 in the equation.
optionRationale.4: This inverts the ratio and uses 2/5 instead of 5/2.

questions.stem: Which of the following oxides is acidic in nature?
questions.explanation: The acidity of the oxides of a transition metal rises with its oxidation state. Manganese in $\text{Mn}_2\text{O}_7$ is in the +7 state, so the oxide is acidic and gives permanganic acid with water. The lower oxides MnO and CrO are basic and $\text{Mn}_3\text{O}_4$ is amphoteric.

optionRationale.1: It is a basic oxide because manganese is in the low +2 state.
optionRationale.3: It is a basic oxide of Cr in the +2 state.

questions.objective: Relate acidic character of oxides to oxidation state

questions.stem: $\text{KMnO}_4$ is not acidified with hydrochloric acid in titrations because
options: hydrochloric acid is too weak to provide $\text{H}^+$ ions
permanganate oxidises chloride ion to chlorine, so some of it is wasted
permanganate is reduced to $\text{MnO}_2$ in the presence of chloride
chloride forms an insoluble precipitate with $\text{Mn}^{2+}$
questions.explanation: In acidic medium $\text{MnO}_4^-$ is a very strong oxidant and also oxidises $\text{Cl}^-$ to $\text{Cl}_2$: $2\text{MnO}_4^- + 16\text{H}^+ + 10\text{Cl}^- \rightarrow 2\text{Mn}^{2+} + 5\text{Cl}_2 + 8\text{H}_2\text{O}$. Some permanganate is used up in this side reaction, which gives an error in the titre. Dilute sulphuric acid is therefore used.

optionRationale.1: HCl is a strong acid and fully provides $\text{H}^+$.
optionRationale.3: In acid it is reduced to $\text{Mn}^{2+}$, whatever the acid used.

questions.objective: Explain the choice of acid for permanganate titrations

questions.stem:
Consider the following statements.
A. $\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7^{2-}$ is orange and $\text{CrO}_4^{2-}$ is yellow, and one changes into the other on changing the pH.
B. In acid solution dichromate oxidises $\text{Fe}^{2+}$ to $\text{Fe}^{3+}$ and is reduced to $\text{Cr}^{3+}$.
C. In acid solution permanganate is reduced to $\text{Mn}^{2+}$, a five-electron change.
D. In neutral solution permanganate is reduced to $\text{Mn}^{2+}$.
Choose the correct answer.
questions.explanation: Chromate (yellow) changes into dichromate (orange) on acidification and back in alkali (A true). Dichromate in acid oxidises $\text{Fe}^{2+}$ and becomes $\text{Cr}^{3+}$ (B true). In acid $\text{MnO}_4^-$ takes five electrons to give $\text{Mn}^{2+}$ (C true). In neutral medium it takes three electrons and gives brown $\text{MnO}_2$, not $\text{Mn}^{2+}$ (D false).

optionRationale.2: D is false: in neutral solution the product is $\text{MnO}_2$.
optionRationale.3: D is false, and A is true.
optionRationale.4: D is false, and A and B are true.

questions.objective: Evaluate statements on dichromate and permanganate chemistry

questions.stem:
Assertion (A): Interstitial compounds of transition metals are hard and have high melting points.
Reason (R): Interstitial compounds are stoichiometric compounds with a fixed ratio of metal to non-metal atoms.
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).
questions.explanation: Interstitial compounds, formed when small atoms such as C, N or H occupy voids in the metal lattice, are hard, have high melting points and are chemically inert, so A is true. They are, however, generally non-stoichiometric, with no fixed formula, so R is false.

optionRationale.1: R is false, so it cannot explain A.
optionRationale.2: R is false: these compounds are usually non-stoichiometric.
optionRationale.4: A is true; interstitial compounds are hard with high melting points.

questions.objective: Recall the characteristics of interstitial compounds

questions.stem: Which lanthanoid ion is most likely to behave as a strong oxidising agent in aqueous solution?
questions.explanation: Lanthanoids are most stable in the +3 state. $\text{Ce}^{4+}$ has the $4f^0$ configuration but is reduced to $\text{Ce}^{3+}$ with $E^\circ = +1.74$ V, so it is a strong oxidising agent. The three $\text{Ln}^{3+}$ ions are already in the stable common state with $4f^0$, $4f^7$ and $4f^{14}$ arrangements.

optionRationale.1: La$^{3+}$ ($4f^0$) is the stable +3 ion and is not an oxidising agent.
optionRationale.2: Lu$^{3+}$ ($4f^{14}$) is the stable +3 ion and has no tendency to be reduced.
optionRationale.3: Gd$^{3+}$ ($4f^7$) is stable in the +3 state and not an oxidant.

questions.objective: Identify the oxidising lanthanoid ion

questions.stem: Which of the following is a feature of the actinoid series but not of the lanthanoid series as a whole?
options: There is a steady decrease in size along the series
Every member of the series is radioactive
Most of the ions are coloured
questions.explanation: Both series show $+3$, a contraction in size across the series and coloured ions. What distinguishes the actinoids is that all of them are radioactive; among the lanthanoids only promethium is radioactive. The actinoids also show a wider range of oxidation states.

optionRationale.1: Both series have +3 as a common oxidation state.
optionRationale.2: Both series show a contraction (the lanthanoid and actinoid contraction).

questions.objective: Compare actinoids and lanthanoids

questions.explanation: The Haber process uses iron with a molybdenum promoter (A-III), the contact process uses $\text{V}_2\text{O}_5$ (B-I), nickel catalyses hydrogenation of oils (C-II) and the Ziegler-Natta catalyst is $\text{TiCl}_4$ with triethylaluminium (D-IV).

optionRationale.2: B and C are interchanged and A, B do not match.

questions.stem: Given $E^\circ(\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7^{2-}/\text{Cr}^{3+}) = +1.33$ V and $E^\circ(\text{Fe}^{3+}/\text{Fe}^{2+}) = +0.77$ V, the $\Delta G^\circ$ for $\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7^{2-} + 14\text{H}^+ + 6\text{Fe}^{2+} \rightarrow 2\text{Cr}^{3+} + 6\text{Fe}^{3+} + 7\text{H}_2\text{O}$ is ($F = 96500$ C mol$^{-1}$)
questions.explanation: $E^\circ_{cell} = 1.33 - 0.77 = 0.56$ V. The balanced equation transfers six electrons, so $n = 6$. $\Delta G^\circ = -nFE^\circ = -6\times96500\times0.56 = -3.24\times10^{5}$ J, that is, $-324$ kJ per mole of reaction.

optionRationale.4: This takes 12 electrons, counting each chromium atom as six.

questions.objective: Calculate Gibbs energy change from electrode potentials
